summary:
Hassan El Mghari opens by framing his talk around preventing AI agents from shipping ugly UIs. He has shipped roughly ten apps a year for five years, some reaching millions of users, and attributes that reach primarily to design and UX rather than to engineering skill, despite not being a trained designer. He briefly promotes Together AI as a cloud platform for running open-source chat, image, audio, and vision models, fine-tuning, and reserving H100/B200 GPU clusters.

He walks through a portfolio of simple one-page apps: a logo creator (about 85,000 users), Make Comics (live at the Together AI booth with an iPad that prints a real comic), a video subtitle generator (about 8,000 users), an open-source AI chat UI, a landing-page variation generator, and an AI cloud agent that spins up sandboxes and opens pull requests. The throughline is that these are deliberately simple apps that lean on design and animation.

El Mghari then names the recognizable tells of "vibe coded" apps: purple gradient backgrounds, italics in headers, a "scroll to explore" prompt, all-caps pills with wide letter spacing, gradient logos, excessive emoji, and padding issues. He argues that once you can list 20–30 of these tells, you can encode them as "slop gates." That idea powers Hallmark, his design skill launched about six weeks before the talk, which has reached more than 10,000 users. Hallmark codifies anti-slop gates and supplies a library of themes as inspiration. Hallmark-generated landing pages are shown as before/after examples, presented as one-shot outputs that still serve as a base for iteration.

For iteration, he prefers a smaller open-source model, GLM 5.2, after starting a base in Codex or Claude Code. He runs a guessing game between GLM 5.2 and Opus 4.8 outputs; most attendees cannot tell them apart, and in one pair the Opus page arguably looks more AI-generated. He closes with a stack of practical habits: maintain a vault of admired UI screenshots and paste them in as references; record voice notes and let prompts run two to three paragraphs; send one or two features per prompt rather than bundling seven; write accumulated do/don't preferences into an AGENTS.md or skills file; prefer cheaper open-source models like GLM 5.2 or Cursor's Composer 2.5 for iteration because they feel magical in speed; and finally, treat every agent output as a base, not a finished app, and keep iterating.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: About 10–20% extra focus on UI/UX is a major competitive advantage for AI apps, even for non-designers.
Recognizable 'vibe coded' tells include purple gradient backgrounds, italicized headers, 'scroll to explore' prompts, all-caps spaced-out pills, gradient logos, and emoji overuse.
Hallmark ships two mechanisms: anti-slop gates plus a curated theme library used as in-context inspiration.
Maintain a vault of admired UI screenshots and paste them into prompts; references and inspiration consistently produce much better output than blank prompts.
Use longer, more specific voice-note prompts of two to three paragraphs, but split work into one or two features per prompt rather than bundling seven.
Maintain a running AGENTS.md or skills file that accumulates do/don't design preferences over time.
Iterate with cheaper open-source models like GLM 5.2 or Cursor's Composer 2.5; treat every agent output as a base, not a finished app.
GLM 5.2 and Opus 4.8 outputs were nearly indistinguishable in a live audience test, while Opus cost about 5x more.
Identify the common visual tells that mark a vibe coded app.
Encode anti-slop rules as explicit gates for an AI agent, or borrow Hallmark.

sections.title: Intro: why design is the edge for AI apps
sections.summary: Hassan introduces himself as dev-ex lead at Together AI, frames the talk as 'stop letting your agents ship ugly UIs,' and notes he ships about 10 apps a year for 5 years, some reaching millions of users, crediting design and UX despite not being a trained designer. He also briefly pitches Together AI's inference, fine-tuning, and GPU cluster offerings across chat, image, audio, and vision modalities.

sections.title: Demo reel: simple one-page apps
sections.summary: Walks through a portfolio of deliberately simple one-page apps: a logo creator (~85,000 users), Make Comics (live at the Together AI booth with an iPad that prints a real comic), a video subtitle generator (~8,000 users), an open-source AI chat UI, a landing-page variation generator, and an AI cloud agent that opens pull requests from a GitHub repo. The point is that small apps with strong design reach real users.

sections.title: The tells of vibe coded apps and Hallmark
sections.summary: Names the recognizable AI slop tells (purple gradients, italic headers, 'scroll to explore,' all-caps spaced-out pills, gradient logos, emoji, padding issues) and argues that listing 20–30 of them lets you encode them as slop gates. Introduces Hallmark, a design skill shipped about six weeks earlier with 10,000+ users, that combines slop gates with a curated theme library used as in-context inspiration. Shows Hallmark landing pages for an indie podcast, an invoicing app, and a before/after for a kids learning app, framing results as one-shot bases rather than finished apps.

sections.title: Iterating with a smaller open-source model
sections.summary: Argues for underused small open-source models in the iteration loop. Starts a base in Codex or Claude Code, then iterates with GLM 5.2 (released about two weeks prior). Runs a live guessing game between GLM 5.2 and Opus 4.8 landing pages; the room is mostly wrong, and the Opus page is sometimes more 'AI looking.' Notes GLM 5.2 was cheaper and faster, with an Opus page costing about 5x as much. Shows a GLM 5.2 one-shot image-playground site cleaned up in 1–2 follow-up prompts.

sections.title: Takeaways: preferences, references, and voice-note prompts
sections.summary: Goal is to beat pure AI slop, not to outcompete professional designers. Key advice: learn the AI tells so you can ask models to avoid them, save accumulated preferences to a skills file or AGENTS.md (or borrow Hallmark if you do not have your own), and treat the agent's first output as a base.

sections.title: Final tips: screenshot vault, scoped prompts, and iterating as a habit
sections.summary: Stresses giving agents references and screenshots from a personal inspiration vault of admired websites and apps, often describing a hybrid look (e.g., 'mix of Duolingo and this app'). Recommends longer, more specific voice-note prompts that run two to three minutes and yield two-to-three-paragraph text prompts, but to break work into one or two features per prompt rather than seven. Notes cheaper open-source models like GLM 5.2 and Cursor's Composer 2.5 feel magical for iteration due to speed. Closes by urging viewers not to one-shot and ship: whatever the agent produces is only the base, and iteration with additional context and inspiration is what makes apps look and feel good.

organization.name: Together AI
organization.summary: Together AI is an independent AI-native cloud that sells serverless, batch, and dedicated inference for open-source models, plus fine-tuning and reserved GPU clusters (H100/B200). Its homepage and products page describe a research-optimized platform for inference, model shaping, and pre-training. Official docs at docs.together.ai cover an OpenAI-compatible API, serverless catalogs, and GPU-cluster launch. The togethercomputer GitHub org publishes official Python and TypeScript SDKs. Hassan El Mghari leads Developer Experience there and presented design-taste / Hallmark habits from this affiliation; the talk's GLM 5.2 iteration loop is the same OSS-inference surface.
organization.status: Live first-party site at together.ai with products, serverless inference, docs.together.ai, api.together.ai/api.together.xyz, and official togethercomputer SDKs as of the research date.
